lead: Thermodynamics can describe a gas in two ways. The microscopic approach follows the molecules: their positions, speeds and collisions, averaged with statistics. The macroscopic approach ignores single molecules and works with a few quantities a gauge or a thermometer can read: pressure p, volume V and temperature T. Engineering thermodynamics uses the macroscopic approach, and it rests on one assumption, the continuum: matter is treated as spread smoothly through space, so every small region has one density, one pressure and one temperature. This chapter shows why that works for a car tyre or a boiler drum and when it stops working.
prereq: You need: school physics ideas of force, pressure, energy and density. Systems and properties are defined in the next two chapters.

sections.h3: Two ways to describe the same gas

blocks.text: Take the air in a closed room. The microscopic approach (also called the statistical view) sees about 10²⁵ molecules in every cubic metre, each moving at a few hundred metres per second and colliding billions of times a second. It cannot follow each one, so it uses probability and averages.

The macroscopic approach (also called the classical view) treats the same air as a body with a handful of measurable properties: pressure p, volume V, temperature T, mass m and density ρ. It never asks what one molecule is doing. Its laws come from experiments on bulk matter.

blocks.text: The two are not rival theories. The microscopic view explains the meaning of the macroscopic quantities; the macroscopic view gives numbers you can design with.

sections.h3: From molecules to pressure and temperature

blocks.text: The link between the two views is an average. Pressure is the average rate at which molecules hand momentum to a wall, per unit area of wall. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the random molecular motion. A gauge on a tank cannot feel one molecule; it reads the steady average of an enormous number of impacts.

sections.h3: The continuum and when it fails

blocks.text: Density at a point is defined by shrinking a small volume δV around the point and dividing the mass inside by the volume: ρ = lim δm/δV as δV shrinks towards δV′, the smallest volume that still holds enough molecules for a steady average. Below δV′ the count of molecules inside jumps up and down as molecules wander in and out, so δm/δV jumps too. Above it, the reading settles to one value. The continuum assumption says every region we care about is much larger than δV′, so properties vary smoothly from point to point and we can use calculus on them.
The size of the scatter follows from statistics: a cube holding N molecules on average gives a count that varies by about √N, a relative spread of 1/√N. Figure 1.1.1 plots this spread for room air.

The continuum fails when the length L of the region (a pipe diameter, a gap, a sensor) is not much larger than the mean free path. The ratio is the Knudsen number, Kn = λ / L. A common rule of thumb: Kn below about 0.01 means the continuum holds; Kn near 1 or above means the molecules hit the walls about as often as each other, and kinetic theory is needed. Vacuum chambers, the thin upper atmosphere and micro-channels are the usual cases.

figure.caption: Room air at 300 K and 101.325 kPa, sampled with cubes of shrinking size. The shaded band is the spread ρ(1 ± 1/√N) for N molecules in the cube: above about 1 µm every cube gives the same density, so the continuum holds; near 10 nm the reading jumps by about 20 %.

spec.aria: A plot of measured density against cube side from 10 nanometres to 10 micrometres. A shaded band is wide on the left, about 20 percent at 10 nm, and shrinks to a thin line at the continuum value 1.177 kilograms per cubic metre on the right. A dotted line marks the mean free path, 67 nm.

examples.question: Air in a room is at 27 °C and 101.325 kPa. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) for air and an effective molecular diameter d = 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find (a) the density from the macroscopic relation ρ = p/(RT), (b) the number of molecules in 1 cm³, (c) the mean free path, and (d) the Knudsen number for a pipe of diameter 10 mm. Can the air in the pipe be treated as a continuum?
steps: Absolute temperature: T = 27 + 273.15 = 300.15 K; use T = 300 K, which changes no answer at three figures.
(a) ρ = p/(RT) = 101.325 kPa ÷ (0.287 kJ/(kg·K) × 300 K) = 101.325 ÷ 86.1 = 1.177 kg/m³. The units work because kPa = kJ/m³.
1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 cm³ holds 2.446 × 10²⁵ × 10⁻⁶ = 2.45 × 10¹⁹ molecules.
Kn is far below 0.01, so the air in the pipe is a continuum: p, ρ and T have one value at each point and the macroscopic approach applies.
examples.answer: ρ = 1.177 kg/m³; 2.45 × 10¹⁹ molecules per cm³; λ ≈ 67 nm; Kn ≈ 6.7 × 10⁻⁶, so the continuum assumption holds.

examples.question: The same air is pumped down in a vacuum chamber to 1.0 Pa at 300 K and flows through a 10 mm tube. Find λ and Kn, and say whether the continuum still holds.
steps: λ is inversely proportional to p at fixed T, so λ = 6.72 × 10⁻⁸ m × (101 325 Pa ÷ 1.0 Pa) = 6.81 × 10⁻³ m = 6.8 mm.

Kn is close to 1, far above 0.01. A molecule crosses most of the tube before it meets another molecule, so a local density or pressure at a point is not well defined. The continuum fails; this flow needs the microscopic (kinetic) treatment.
examples.answer: λ ≈ 6.8 mm and Kn ≈ 0.68: the continuum assumption fails in the evacuated tube.

traps: Pressure is caused by molecular impacts, but it is a macroscopic property: a gauge reads the average of an enormous number of impacts, never one molecule.
The continuum is not about the size of the object alone. A 10 mm tube is a continuum at 101 kPa (Kn ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶) but not at 1 Pa (Kn ≈ 0.7): pressure matters through λ.
Use absolute temperature in K and absolute pressure in Pa in n = p/(kT) and λ = kT/(√2 π d² p). Writing 27 °C for T gives an answer eleven times too large.
Do not say the two approaches give different laws. They describe the same state; the macroscopic laws can be derived from the microscopic model, and they agree.

quiz.q: Define the macroscopic approach to thermodynamics.
quiz.a: It studies matter through a few bulk properties that instruments measure, such as p, V and T, without following individual molecules.
Matter is treated as continuous, so properties such as density, pressure and temperature have one value at each point and vary smoothly from point to point.

quiz.q: Why does engineering design use the macroscopic approach?
quiz.a: A sample holds about 10²⁵ molecules per m³, far too many to follow. A few measurable properties are enough to calculate heat, work and energy changes, which is what design needs.

quiz.q: Find the density of air at 200 kPa and 400 K, with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K).
Air at 300 K has λ = 67 nm at 101.325 kPa. Find λ and Kn for a 0.10 mm gap at 101.325 kPa.
quiz.a: λ stays 67 nm at the same p and T. Kn = 6.7 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.7 × 10⁻⁴, below 0.01, so the continuum still holds in the gap.

quiz.q: A probe measures the average molecular speed in a cube 10 nm on a side; a gauge measures the pressure of the whole tank. Which reading is a macroscopic property, and why does the probe's reading jump?
quiz.a: The tank pressure is macroscopic. A 10 nm cube of room air holds only about 24 molecules on average, so the count, and any average over it, changes by about 1/√24 ≈ 20 % as molecules move in and out.

beyond: Rarefied gas dynamics uses the Boltzmann equation and direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) where the continuum fails, for example for satellites in low orbit and for flows in micro-electro-mechanical devices. Molecular dynamics simulates atoms directly and feeds averaged properties to continuum solvers. Statistical thermodynamics derives the ideal-gas law and specific heats from the molecular model.
